questions.prompt: What does `new C()` return?

choices.text: the allocated instance, with n equal to 1

query.title: An object return replaces the new instance
query.syntax: new C(); // { n: 2 }, not the instance
query.explanation: If a constructor returns an object, `new` returns that object and drops the instance it allocated. The assignment `this.n = 1` still runs, but the caller never receives that instance. A primitive return would not replace the instance, and the returned object is not unwrapped to `2`.

questions.prompt: What does `new C()` return?

choices.text: the allocated instance, with n equal to 1

query.title: A primitive return keeps the instance
query.explanation: A constructor return value replaces the allocated instance only when that value is an object. `2` is a primitive, so `new` ignores it and returns the instance whose `n` is `1`. The expression does not evaluate to `2`, and returning a primitive is not a TypeError.

questions.prompt: What is `steps` after `new C()`?

query.title: Field initializers run before the constructor body
query.explanation: On a base class, public field initializers run on the new instance before the constructor body. `steps` is therefore `["field", "body"]`. The constructor body does not run first, and the field initializer is not deferred until after the constructor returns.

questions.prompt: What is `new C().b`?

query.title: A later field can read an earlier field
query.explanation: Public fields initialize in source order, so `a` is already `1` when the `b` initializer reads `this.a`. `b` is `2`. The later initializer does not see `a` as missing, and the read is not a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: What happens when `new C()` runs?

choices.text: an instance with a undefined and b equal to 1
an instance with a and b both equal to 1

query.title: An earlier field reads a later field as undefined
query.syntax:
class C { a = this.b; b = 1; }
new C(); // { a: undefined, b: 1 }
query.explanation: Public fields initialize in source order. `this.b` during the `a` initializer does not throw and does not see the later value `1`; the property is not initialized yet, so the read is `undefined` and `b` is then set to `1`. A bare `b` (with no `this`) would be a different error: that name is not a lexical binding and throws ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: What is `steps` after `new C()`?

query.title: Derived fields initialize when super returns
query.syntax: new C(); // before, super, field, after
query.explanation: In a derived class, public fields initialize immediately after `super()` returns and before the rest of the constructor body. The order is `before`, `super`, `field`, `after`. Fields do not run before `super()`, and they do not wait until the constructor returns.

questions.prompt: What is `steps` after the class declaration is evaluated?

query.title: Static fields run during class evaluation
query.syntax: class C { static a = ...; static b = ...; } // a then b
query.explanation: Static public fields initialize while the class is evaluated, in source order, so `steps` is `["a", "b"]` as soon as the declaration finishes. They do not wait for `new C()`, and a later static field does not run before an earlier one.

questions.prompt: What is `steps` after `class C` is evaluated?

query.title: The base class finishes before the subclass body
query.syntax: class C extends class { static x } { static y } // base, then sub
query.explanation: The `extends` expression is evaluated to completion, including the base class static fields, before the subclass body runs. `steps` is `["base", "sub"]`. The subclass static field does not run first, and the base static field is not skipped.

questions.prompt: What does calling the class as a function do?
questions.code:
class C {}
C();

query.title: A class constructor requires new
query.explanation: A class constructor can only be invoked with `new`. Calling `C()` throws a TypeError. It does not return `undefined` or an instance, and the failure is not a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: What is `seen === S` after `new S()`?

query.title: new.target is the constructed subclass
query.syntax: new S(); // new.target inside B is S
query.explanation: `new.target` is the function that `new` was applied to, not the class whose constructor body is running. `new S()` therefore sets `new.target` to `S` even while the base constructor is running. It is not `B`, and it is not `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What is `steps` after `class C` is evaluated?

query.title: extends is evaluated before the class body
query.syntax: class C extends getBase() { static y } // extends, then body
query.explanation: The `extends` expression runs before any part of the class body, including static field initializers. `steps` is `["extends", "body"]`. The class body does not start first, and the heritage expression is not deferred until the first `new`.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true of `class C extends null`?

choices.text: C.prototype has a null [[Prototype]], and super() throws TypeError
C.prototype inherits from Object.prototype, and super() returns the instance
C.prototype has a null [[Prototype]], and super() returns the instance
the class declaration is a SyntaxError

query.title: extends null has no prototype parent
query.syntax:
class C extends null {}
Object.getPrototypeOf(C.prototype); // null
query.explanation: `extends null` sets the [[Prototype]] of `C.prototype` to null, and the class declaration itself is legal. Calling `super()` then throws a TypeError because null is not a constructor. `super()` does not return the instance, and `C.prototype` does not inherit from `Object.prototype`.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.keys(C.prototype)` return?

query.title: Class methods are non-enumerable
query.explanation: Methods defined in a class body are non-enumerable, so `Object.keys` does not list `m` or `constructor`. The method is still an own property of the prototype; it is only hidden from enumerable enumeration. The call does not throw.

questions.prompt: What is `1 instanceof C`?

query.title: Symbol.hasInstance customizes instanceof
query.syntax: 1 instanceof C; // true when hasInstance says so
query.explanation: `instanceof` calls a `Symbol.hasInstance` method on the right-hand constructor when one exists, and uses that boolean result. Here the method returns true only for `1`, so `1 instanceof C` is true. The ordinary prototype-chain test is not used, and a custom method does not throw by itself.

questions.prompt: What is `f.bind(null, 1).length`?
questions.code:
function f(a, b) {}
f.bind(null, 1).length;

query.title: bind reduces length by the bound arguments
query.explanation: `length` counts parameters that are not already supplied by `bind`. Binding one argument of `(a, b)` leaves one unbound parameter, so `length` is `1`. It does not stay `2`, and it does not drop to `0` unless every parameter was bound.

questions.prompt: What is `f.bind(null).prototype`?
questions.code:
function f() {}
f.bind(null).prototype;

query.title: A bound function has no prototype property
query.explanation: A bound function does not get its own `prototype` property, so reading it yields `undefined`. `bind` does not copy `f.prototype` and does not allocate a fresh prototype object. The value is `undefined`, not `null`.

questions.prompt: What does `outer()` do?

query.title: new Function does not close over locals
query.explanation: A function created by `new Function` is compiled as top-level code in the global scope. It does not close over `const x` inside `outer`, so `return x` throws a ReferenceError. It does not return `1` or `undefined`. A bare top-level `const x` in a classic script is a different case: that binding is global, and `new Function` can see it.

questions.prompt: What is `this` inside `f` when `f()` is called as a bare call?
questions.code:
const f = new Function("return this;");
f();

query.title: new Function is sloppy unless the source is strict
query.explanation: Code compiled by `new Function` is sloppy unless that source itself enables strict mode. A bare call therefore sets `this` to the global object. A `"use strict"` directive in the source would make `this` undefined, but that directive is absent here, so the value is not `undefined` or `null`.

questions.prompt: What does `f(1)` return?

query.title: Strict arguments do not alias parameters
query.explanation: In strict mode, the `arguments` object does not alias the named parameters. Writing `arguments[0]` leaves `a` at `1`. The assignment does not update the parameter to `9`, and it does not throw.

questions.prompt: What does `f(1)` return?

query.title: Sloppy arguments alias the named parameter
query.explanation: A function created by `new Function` is sloppy unless its source turns on strict mode. In a sloppy function, assigning `arguments[0]` also assigns the matching named parameter, so `a` becomes `9`. Strict mode would have left `a` at `1`, and the assignment does not throw.

questions.prompt: What is `this` for `fn.call(null)` in each mode?

choices.text: strict: null; sloppy: the global object
strict: the global object; sloppy: null

query.title: call(null) is not rewritten in strict mode
query.explanation: `call` passes its first argument through as `this`. Strict mode keeps that value, so `this` is `null`. A sloppy function replaces `null` or `undefined` with the global object. Strict mode does not turn `null` into `undefined`, and the sloppy call does not keep `null`.

questions.prompt: What does `f()` return?

query.title: Strict direct eval does not leak var
query.explanation: A direct `eval` in strict mode creates its `var` bindings in the eval scope only. Those bindings do not leak into the caller, so `typeof x` is `"undefined"`. The declaration is not a SyntaxError, and `x` is not a number in `f`.

questions.prompt: What does calling `f` do?

query.title: A body let cannot reuse a parameter name
query.explanation: Parameter defaults are evaluated in a scope outside the function body, but a `let` in that body still cannot repeat a parameter name. The declaration is a SyntaxError before `f` can be called. The call does not return `2` or `1`.

questions.prompt: What does `f()` do?

query.title: A default cannot read a later parameter
query.syntax:
function f(a = b, b = 2) { return a; }
f(); // ReferenceError
query.explanation: Parameter defaults are evaluated left to right, and each parameter is in the temporal dead zone until its own initializer finishes. `a` reads `b` before `b` is initialized, so the call throws a ReferenceError. `a` does not become `2` or `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What are the first two `g.next()` results?

query.title: yield* yields values, then returns the inner result
query.syntax: yield* inner(); yield value; // 1, then 9, both done false
query.explanation: `yield*` yields each value the inner iterator yields, so the first `next` is `{value:1, done:false}`. The `yield*` expression then becomes the inner iterator return value, `9`, and the outer `yield value` produces `{value:9, done:false}`. That second result is not done, because the outer generator yielded it rather than completing.

questions.prompt: What does `it.throw(new Error("boom"))` return?

choices.text: the exception escapes and the generator stays paused

query.title: throw injects an exception at the paused yield
query.explanation: `generator.throw` resumes the generator by throwing at the paused `yield`, so the `catch` runs and returns `"boom"`. The result is `{value:"boom", done:true}`. The exception does not escape an active `catch`, and the generator does not stay paused on `1`.

questions.prompt: What are `result` and `steps` after `it.return(7)`?

choices.text: result is {value:7, done:true}, and steps is ["fin"]
result is {value:7, done:true}, and steps is []
result is {value:1, done:true}, and steps is ["fin"]
result is {value:undefined, done:true}, and steps is ["fin"]

query.title: return completes the generator and runs finally
query.explanation: `generator.return(7)` completes the generator with `{value:7, done:true}`. A `finally` wrapped around the paused `yield` still runs, so `steps` is `["fin"]`. The completion value stays `7` rather than becoming `1` or `undefined`, and `finally` is not skipped.

questions.prompt: What does the promise from `f()` fulfill with?

query.title: An async return adopts a thenable
query.syntax: async () => thenable; // fulfills with 5, not the thenable
query.explanation: When an async function returns a thenable, it adopts that thenable instead of fulfilling with the thenable object. `then` calls `resolve(5)`, so the promise fulfills with `5`. The fulfillment value is not the thenable itself, and a resolving `then` does not reject.

questions.prompt: What is `steps` immediately after `new Promise` returns, before any await?

query.title: The promise executor runs synchronously
query.syntax:
new Promise(() => steps.push("exec"));
steps.push("after"); // exec, after
query.explanation: The executor passed to `new Promise` runs synchronously, before `new Promise` returns. `steps` is `["exec", "after"]` on the next line. The executor is not deferred as a microtask, and `"after"` is not pushed before `"exec"`.

questions.prompt: What does the promise fulfill with?

query.title: A second resolve is ignored
query.explanation: The first call to the executor `resolve` function settles the promise. A later call does not change it, so the promise fulfills with `1`. The second value does not win, and calling `resolve` twice does not reject.

questions.prompt: What is `Promise.resolve(p) === p`?
questions.code:
const p = Promise.resolve(1);
Promise.resolve(p) === p;

choices.text: false, because resolve always wraps its argument
true only after p is already fulfilled

query.title: Promise.resolve returns a native promise unchanged
query.syntax:
const p = Promise.resolve(1);
Promise.resolve(p) === p; // true
query.explanation: `Promise.resolve` returns an existing native promise as the same object. It does not wrap `p` in a second promise, and it does not throw. The identity holds because `p` is already a built-in promise, not because of its fulfillment state.

questions.prompt: What does `p` fulfill with?

query.title: Promise.resolve adopts a thenable
query.explanation: `Promise.resolve` on a thenable adopts it by calling `then`, so `p` fulfills with `4`. `p` is a new promise, not the thenable object, and the fulfillment value is not the thenable. A `then` that resolves does not reject.

questions.prompt: What happens to `p`?

query.title: A throwing then rejects the adopting promise
query.syntax: Promise.resolve({ then() { throw new Error("sync"); } }); // rejects
query.explanation: If the thenable `then` throws synchronously, the promise that adopted it rejects with that error. `Promise.resolve` itself does not let the exception escape, and `p` does not fulfill or stay pending. The rejection is how the throw is captured.

questions.prompt: After the microtask queue drains, what is `order`?

query.title: A microtask queued inside then runs after queued jobs
query.syntax: first then, second then, then the inner microtask
query.explanation: Both `then` callbacks are already queued, so they run in queue order: `first`, then `second`. The microtask queued inside the first callback is appended behind jobs that were already queued, so `inner` is last. The inner job does not jump ahead of `second`.

questions.prompt: What does `JSON.stringify(-0)` return?
questions.code: JSON.stringify(-0);

query.title: JSON.stringify writes -0 as 0
query.explanation: JSON has no distinct negative zero, so `JSON.stringify(-0)` returns the string `"0"`. It does not preserve the sign as `"-0"`. The result is a string, not the number `0`, and it is not `null` (that is what `JSON.stringify` does with `NaN` and infinities).

questions.prompt: What does `JSON.stringify(1n)` do?
questions.code: JSON.stringify(1n);

query.title: JSON.stringify rejects bigint
query.explanation: JSON has no bigint type, and `JSON.stringify` throws a TypeError when it meets one. It does not coerce the value to `"1"` or `"1n"`. A bigint is not an unsupported value that is omitted as `undefined`; the throw happens when the bigint itself is being serialized.

questions.prompt: What does `JSON.stringify(o)` do?

query.title: JSON.stringify rejects a cycle
query.explanation: `JSON.stringify` throws a TypeError when it walks a circular structure. It does not drop the cycle and return `"{}"`, and it does not replace the back-reference with `null`. The failure is a throw, not an `undefined` return.

questions.prompt: What does `JSON.stringify` return?

query.title: toJSON replaces the object being serialized
query.explanation: If an object has `toJSON`, `JSON.stringify` serializes the return value of `toJSON` instead of the object own properties. The result is `"{\"n\":1}"`. The `x` property is not emitted, and a `toJSON` method is not a TypeError.

questions.prompt: What is `seen` after the parse?

query.title: A reviver sees children before the parent
query.explanation: A `JSON.parse` reviver walks bottom-up: each child property is visited before its parent object, and the root is last with the empty-string key. `seen` is `["b", "a", ""]`. The root is not first, and a parent is not visited before its children.

questions.prompt: What is `clone.self === clone`?

choices.text: false, because the cycle is dropped
true, and clone is a different object from o
false, because structuredClone throws on a cycle

query.title: structuredClone preserves a cycle
query.syntax: clone.self === clone; // true, and clone !== o
query.explanation: `structuredClone` preserves a cycle, so the clone points at itself the same way the original does. `clone.self === clone` is true, and `clone` is not the original object. The algorithm does not throw on this cycle and does not drop `self`.

questions.prompt: What is true of `structuredClone(new Map([[1, 2]]))`?
questions.code: const clone = structuredClone(new Map([[1, 2]]));

choices.text: it is a Map whose get(1) is 2
it is an array of pairs

query.title: structuredClone keeps a Map as a Map
query.explanation: `structuredClone` of a Map returns a Map, and the entries are copied, so `get(1)` is `2`. The clone is not a plain object and not an array of pairs. A Map is a supported clone type, so this value does not throw.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what does the assignment do?

choices.text: the target gains an own property x
the assignment expression evaluates to false

query.title: A false set trap throws in strict mode
query.syntax:
"use strict";
p.x = 1; // TypeError when set returns false
query.explanation: In strict mode, a Proxy `set` trap that returns false causes the assignment to throw a TypeError. The assignment is not ignored, and the target does not gain `x`. The failure is a throw, not a false completion value.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what does `delete p.a` do?

choices.text: returns false and leaves a in place

query.title: A false deleteProperty trap throws in strict mode
query.syntax:
"use strict";
delete p.a; // TypeError when the trap returns false
query.explanation: In strict mode, a Proxy `deleteProperty` trap that returns false causes `delete` to throw a TypeError. The operator does not return false and leave the property, and it does not remove `a`. The result is not `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What does reading `p.a` do?

query.title: A get trap must honor a frozen data property
query.syntax: p.a; // TypeError, the trap returned 2 instead of 1
query.explanation: If a target data property is non-configurable and non-writable, the `get` trap must return that property actual value. Returning `2` instead of `1` makes the get throw a TypeError. The read does not produce `2` or fall through to `1`.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what does `o.a = 2` do?

choices.text: leaves a at 1 and does not throw

query.title: Strict assignment to a non-writable property throws
query.explanation: In strict mode, assigning to a non-writable own data property throws a TypeError. The property does not stay `1` by silently ignoring the write, and it does not become `2`. The failure is a TypeError, not a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what does `o.a = 2` do?

choices.text: leaves a at 1 and does not throw

query.title: Strict assignment to a frozen object throws
query.explanation: In strict mode, assigning to a property of an `Object.freeze`d object throws a TypeError. The frozen property does not ignore the write, and it does not change to `2`. The failure is a TypeError, not a SyntaxError.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what does `delete o.a` do?

query.title: Strict delete on a sealed object throws
query.explanation: In strict mode, `delete` of an existing property on an `Object.seal`ed object throws a TypeError. The property is non-configurable, so the delete does not return false and leave it, and it does not remove `a`. The result is not `undefined`.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what does `o.a = 1` do?

choices.text: leaves a undefined and does not throw

query.title: Strict assignment cannot extend a non-extensible object
query.explanation: In strict mode, adding a property after `Object.preventExtensions` throws a TypeError. The new property is not created, and the failed add is not silent. The failure is a TypeError, not a SyntaxError.

questions.prompt: What is `[typeof (d + 1), typeof (d - 1)]`?
questions.code:
const d = new Date(0);
[typeof (d + 1), typeof (d - 1)];

query.title: Date addition concatenates and subtraction subtracts
query.explanation: A Date plus a number converts the Date with its default hint, which prefers `toString`, so `+` concatenates and the result is a string. A Date minus a number uses numeric conversion, so the result is a number. The two operators do not both produce numbers or both produce strings.

questions.prompt: For an ordinary object, which ToPrimitive order is correct?

choices.text: number hint: valueOf then toString; string hint: toString then valueOf
number hint: toString then valueOf; string hint: valueOf then toString

query.title: Ordinary ToPrimitive swaps order by hint
query.syntax:
o + 1; // 3, from valueOf
String(o); // "3", from toString
query.explanation: Ordinary ToPrimitive tries `valueOf` before `toString` for a number hint, and `toString` before `valueOf` for a string hint. `o + 1` uses the default hint, which for an ordinary object tries `valueOf` first and becomes `3`, while `String(o)` uses the string hint and becomes `"3"`. The same order is not used for both hints.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.prototype.toString.call(o)` return?
questions.code:
const o = { [Symbol.toStringTag]: "Box" };
Object.prototype.toString.call(o);

query.title: Symbol.toStringTag sets the Object toString tag
query.explanation: `Symbol.toStringTag` changes the tag that `Object.prototype.toString` puts inside `[object ...]`. The call returns `"[object Box]"`. It does not keep the default `"[object Object]"` tag, and it does not return the bare tag string.

questions.prompt: What does `-1 >>> 0` evaluate to?

query.title: Unsigned right shift turns -1 into the uint32 max
query.explanation: `>>>` converts its operand to a uint32 before shifting. The uint32 form of `-1` is `4294967295`, and shifting by `0` leaves that value. The result is not `-1`, and a zero shift does not produce `0`.

questions.prompt: What does `1.9 | 0` evaluate to?

query.title: Bitwise OR truncates toward zero through int32
query.explanation: A bitwise operator converts each operand with ToInt32, which truncates toward zero. `1.9` becomes `1`, and `1 | 0` is `1`. The conversion does not round to `2`, and the original `1.9` is not preserved.

questions.prompt: What is `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2`?
questions.code: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2;

query.title: Both sums collapse to the same float
query.explanation: Past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, IEEE-754 doubles can no longer represent every integer. Both `+ 1` and `+ 2` produce the same value, so the comparison is true. The two sums are not distinct, and the comparison does not throw.

questions.prompt: What does `1 / -0` evaluate to?

query.title: Dividing by negative zero yields -Infinity
query.explanation: Division by zero follows the sign of the zero. `1 / -0` is `-Infinity`. It is not positive `Infinity`, and it is not `NaN` or `0`.

questions.prompt: What are `Math.round(1.5)` and `Math.round(-1.5)`?
questions.code: [Math.round(1.5), Math.round(-1.5)];

query.title: Math.round breaks ties toward +Infinity
query.explanation: `Math.round` rounds a half toward `+Infinity`. `1.5` becomes `2`, and `-1.5` becomes `-1` rather than `-2`. The negative half is not rounded away from zero, and `1.5` is not truncated to `1`.

questions.prompt: What does the mapped index list equal after the sort?

choices.text: an order the spec leaves undefined

query.title: Array sort is stable
query.syntax: items.sort((a, b) => a.k - b.k); // equal keys keep [0, 1, 2]
query.explanation: `Array.prototype.sort` is stable, so elements that compare equal stay in their original order. Every `k` is `1`, and the indexes remain `[0, 1, 2]`. The sort does not reverse equal elements, and their relative order is not left up to the engine.

questions.prompt: What is `[map.size, map.get(+0)]`?

query.title: Map treats +0 and -0 as one key
query.explanation: Map uses SameValueZero, which treats `+0` and `-0` as the same key. The second `set` overwrites the first, `size` stays `1`, and `get(+0)` is `"neg"`. The map does not keep two zero keys.

questions.prompt: What is `[a[1], b[1]]`?

query.title: with returns a new array
query.explanation: `array.with` returns a new array with the index replaced and leaves the receiver unchanged. `a[1]` stays `2` and `b[1]` is `9`. The method does not write through to `a`.

questions.prompt: What does `findLast` return?

query.title: findLast returns the last match
query.explanation: `findLast` walks from the end and returns the last element that matches. Both `2` and `4` are even, so the result is `4`. It does not return the first match, and a match exists so the result is not `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What is `seen` after `reduce`?

query.title: reduce skips holes
query.explanation: `reduce` skips holes and does not invoke the callback for them. The hole at index `1` is absent from `seen`, which is `[0, 2]`. The callback does not run with an `undefined` element for that hole, and it does not visit only the first index.

questions.prompt: What does `copyWithin` return?

query.title: copyWithin copies from a snapshot of the overlap
query.explanation: `copyWithin(2, 0, 3)` copies the range from index `0` through `3` onto index `2`. The overlapping copy is taken from a snapshot, so the result is `[1, 2, 1, 2, 3]`. It does not keep reading values that the copy already overwrote, and the receiver is not left unchanged.

questions.prompt: What is `Array.isArray(new Uint8Array([1]))`?
questions.code: Array.isArray(new Uint8Array([1]));

query.title: A typed array is not an Array
query.explanation: `Array.isArray` is true only for objects whose internal slot marks them as arrays. A `Uint8Array` is a typed array, so the result is false. Indexed access does not make it an array, and the check does not throw.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true?

choices.text: literal uses proto as its prototype, and computed has an own __proto__ property
both objects use proto as their prototype
both objects have an own __proto__ property and neither changes the prototype
literal has an own __proto__ property, and computed uses proto as its prototype

query.title: Only a literal __proto__ key sets the prototype
query.syntax:
{ __proto__: proto }; // sets prototype
{ ["__proto__"]: proto }; // own property
query.explanation: An object-literal `__proto__` key sets the [[Prototype]] and does not create an own property. A computed key `["__proto__"]` creates an own data property and leaves the prototype as `Object.prototype`. The two spellings are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: What does `1n + 1` do?

query.title: BigInt and Number cannot be mixed with +
query.explanation: The `+` operator does not coerce between bigint and number. `1n + 1` throws a TypeError. It does not produce `2n` or `2`, and it does not concatenate the way a string `+` would.

questions.prompt: What is `[typeof 1n, 1n === 1]`?
questions.code: [typeof 1n, 1n === 1];

query.title: bigint has its own typeof and is not === to a number
query.explanation: `typeof 1n` is `"bigint"`, and strict equality does not coerce, so `1n === 1` is false. The typeof tag is not `"number"` or `"object"`. The values are not strictly equal just because both mean one.

questions.prompt: What does `5n / 2n` evaluate to?

query.title: BigInt division truncates toward zero
query.explanation: BigInt division truncates toward zero and stays in bigint, so `5n / 2n` is `2n`. There is no `2.5n`, and the result is not the number `2`. Exact division of integers does not throw.

questions.prompt: What does `+Symbol("s")` do?
questions.code: +Symbol("s");

query.title: Unary plus cannot convert a symbol
query.explanation: Unary plus applies a numeric conversion, and converting a symbol to a number throws a TypeError. The result is not `NaN`, `0`, or a string. Symbols do not coerce the way objects do.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true for `const symbol = Symbol("s")`?
questions.code: const symbol = Symbol("s");

choices.text: symbol + "" throws TypeError, and String(symbol) returns a string
both symbol + "" and String(symbol) throw TypeError
both symbol + "" and String(symbol) return a string
symbol + "" returns a string, and String(symbol) throws TypeError

query.title: String concatenation rejects a symbol, String() does not
query.explanation: Concatenating a symbol with a string throws a TypeError, because the string conversion used by `+` rejects symbols. `String(symbol)` is the explicit conversion and returns a string such as `"Symbol(s)"`. The two operations are not the same, and `String` does not throw.

questions.prompt: What is `[Object.hasOwn(returned, "n"), created.n]`?

query.title: A returned object does not receive the public fields
query.explanation: Public fields are installed on the original `this` after `super()` returns. When the derived constructor returns a different object, that returned object does not have `n`, while the discarded `this` does. The field is not moved onto the returned object, and returning an object is not a TypeError.

questions.prompt: An optional call does not evaluate its arguments when the base is null or undefined.

query.title: Optional call skips the argument list
query.syntax: fn?.(seen = true); // seen stays false when fn is null
query.explanation: When the base of an optional call is null or undefined, the call is skipped and its arguments are not evaluated. `seen` stays false. This is stricter than a normal call, which would evaluate the arguments before discovering that the callee cannot be called.

questions.prompt: `??=` assigns when the left side is null or undefined, and it leaves 0 in place.

query.title: Nullish assignment ignores 0
query.explanation: `??=` assigns only when the left side is null or undefined, so `missing` becomes `5`. `0` is not nullish, so `zero` stays `0`. The operator does not use truthiness, which would have replaced `0` as well.

questions.prompt: `||=` does not assign when the left side is already truthy.

query.title: Logical or assignment keeps a truthy left side
query.explanation: `||=` assigns only when the left side is falsy. `1` is truthy, so `value` stays `1` and the right side is not evaluated. The operator does not overwrite a value that is already truthy.

questions.prompt: The comma operator evaluates both operands and yields the right-hand one.

query.title: The comma operator yields the right operand
query.explanation: The comma operator evaluates the left operand, then the right operand, and its result is the right-hand value. `result` is `2` and `n` is `1`, so the assignment did run. The operator does not skip the left side or yield it.

questions.prompt: An arrow function written at the top level cannot contain `super`; that program is a SyntaxError.
questions.code: const fn = () => super.toString();

query.title: A bare arrow has no super binding
query.explanation: An arrow function does not create a `super` binding of its own. This arrow is not inside a method or constructor, so the `super` keyword is a SyntaxError when the program is parsed. The failure is not a TypeError at the call.

questions.prompt: A sticky regexp (`y` flag) matches only at lastIndex. `/a/y` with lastIndex 0 does not match "xa", and lastIndex stays 0.

query.title: A sticky regexp anchors at lastIndex
query.syntax:
const re = /a/y;
re.exec("xa"); // null, lastIndex stays 0
query.explanation: The `y` flag requires the match to begin at `lastIndex`. At `0`, `"xa"` does not start with `a`, so `exec` returns null and leaves `lastIndex` at `0`. A sticky regexp does not scan forward the way a global regexp does.

questions.prompt: A unicode property escape `\p{L}` without the `u` or `v` flag is a SyntaxError.

query.title: Without u or v, \p is an identity escape
query.explanation: Without the `u` or `v` flag, `\p` is an identity escape, so `/\p{L}/` matches the literal characters p{L}. It is not a SyntaxError, and it does not match letters. The `u` or `v` flag is what turns `\p{L}` into a unicode property escape.

questions.prompt: A tagged template containing an illegal escape throws while the cooked strings are being built.

query.title: A tagged illegal escape cooks to undefined
query.syntax: tag`\unicode`; // called, cooked element is undefined
query.explanation: An illegal escape in a tagged template does not throw while the cooked strings are built. The cooked element is `undefined`, and the tag function is still called with the raw strings available. An untagged template with the same escape is a SyntaxError, which is the case this does not follow.

questions.prompt: `Object.prototype.toString.call(null)` is `"[object Null]"`.
questions.code: Object.prototype.toString.call(null);

query.title: toString tags null as Null
query.explanation: `Object.prototype.toString` special-cases null and returns `"[object Null]"`. It does not throw, and it does not report `"[object Object]"`. The tag names the null value itself.

questions.prompt: Reading `arguments.callee` in strict mode throws TypeError.

query.title: Strict mode hides arguments.callee
query.explanation: In strict mode, reading `arguments.callee` throws a TypeError. The property is not a reference to the running function. Sloppy code could read it, and strict mode removes that access instead of returning `undefined`.

questions.prompt: Indirect eval, `(0, eval)(source)`, does not create bindings in the local scope.

query.title: Indirect eval does not bind locals
query.explanation: Indirect eval runs in the global scope, so `var x = 2` does not create or assign a binding in the local scope. The local `x` stays `1`. The comma operator is what makes the call indirect; the `var` is not installed beside the local `let`.

questions.prompt: A static method can call a base static method with `super.method()`.

query.title: super reaches a base static method
query.syntax:
class C extends B { static m() { return super.m() + 1; } }
C.m(); // 2
query.explanation: A static method has a home object of the constructor, so `super.method()` looks up the base class static method. `C.m()` returns `2`. `super` is not limited to instance methods, and this call does not throw.

questions.prompt: A subclass whose `Symbol.species` is `Array` makes `map` return an Array, not the subclass.

query.title: Symbol.species chooses the map constructor
query.syntax: new MyArray(1, 2).map((n) => n) instanceof MyArray; // false
query.explanation: Array methods that build a derived object consult `Symbol.species`. When that getter returns `Array`, `map` returns an `Array`, so `mapped instanceof MyArray` is false. The method does not always construct the receiver subclass.

questions.prompt: A module namespace object (`import * as ns`) is not extensible.
questions.code:
import * as ns from "./mod.js";
Object.isExtensible(ns);

query.title: A module namespace object is not extensible
query.syntax:
import * as ns from "./mod.js";
Object.isExtensible(ns); // false
query.explanation: A module namespace object is not extensible, so adding a property throws in strict mode and `Object.isExtensible` is false. The namespace is a fixed view of the module exports. It is not an ordinary object that the importer can extend.

questions.prompt: `import()` returns a promise that fulfills with the module namespace.
questions.code: const namespace = await import("./mod.js");

query.title: Dynamic import fulfills with the namespace
query.explanation: `import()` returns a promise, and that promise fulfills with the module namespace object. It does not fulfill with a single default export unless that is read off the namespace. The call is not synchronous.

questions.prompt: A throw inside `finally` replaces an exception that `try` or `catch` was about to propagate.

query.title: A finally throw replaces the pending exception
query.syntax: try { throw new Error("try"); } finally { throw new Error("fin"); } // "fin"
query.explanation: If `finally` throws, that new exception propagates and the exception `try` or `catch` was about to throw is discarded. The caught message is `"fin"`, not `"try"`. `finally` does not throw both or let the original win.

questions.prompt: A `#x` private field in a base class and a `#x` private field in a subclass are different brands.

query.title: Private names are branded per class
query.explanation: Each class has its own private name, even when the source text is `#x` in both. The instance holds both fields, so the base getter returns `1` and the subclass getter returns `2`. The subclass field does not overwrite the base field.

questions.prompt: A static initialization block can read a private static field declared earlier in the same class.

query.title: A static block sees an earlier private static field
query.explanation: Static fields and static blocks run in source order while the class is evaluated. A block that appears after `static #x` can read that private field, so `C.y` is `4`. The private name is in scope for later elements of the same class, and the read does not throw.

questions.prompt: `new Error(message, { cause }).cause` is the cause value, and the cause is not pasted into `message`.

query.title: Error cause is a separate property
query.explanation: The second argument to `Error` may include a `cause`, stored on the `cause` property. The `message` stays `"outer"` and does not gain the cause text. The cause is not only a console detail; it is a real property, and it is not concatenated into `message`.

questions.prompt: An `AggregateError` stores the input reasons on its `errors` array.
questions.code:
const error = new AggregateError([new Error("a"), "b"], "many");
error.errors.length;

query.title: AggregateError keeps an errors array
query.explanation: `AggregateError` stores the iterable of reasons on its `errors` array, in order. The message `"many"` is separate and does not replace those reasons. The reasons are not dropped after the error is constructed.

questions.prompt: `for await...of` consumes an async iterable one element at a time, in order.

query.title: for await...of walks an async iterable in order
query.syntax: for await (const value of gen()) out.push(value); // ["p", "q"]
query.explanation: `for await...of` awaits each next result before taking the following one, so the values arrive in yield order. `out` becomes `["p", "q"]`. The loop does not collect the yields concurrently or reverse them.

questions.prompt: An async generator pauses at `yield` until the consumer calls `next` again.

query.title: An async generator stays paused at yield
query.syntax:
await it.next();
steps; // ["before"] until the next next()
query.explanation: An async generator runs until a `yield`, then pauses. After the first `next`, `steps` is `["before"]` and `"after"` has not run. The code after `yield` waits for the consumer to call `next` again. It does not continue to the second yield on its own.

questions.prompt: `String.prototype.matchAll` requires a global regexp and returns an iterator of match objects.
questions.code: "a1b2".matchAll(/(\d)/g);

query.title: matchAll requires a global regexp
query.explanation: `matchAll` returns an iterator of match objects, and only when the regexp is global. The same pattern without `g` throws a TypeError. The method does not return a single match array the way `match` does for a non-global regexp.

questions.prompt: A named capture group is available as `match.groups.name`.
questions.code:
const match = "ab".match(/(?<name>a)/);
match.groups.name;

query.title: Named groups live on match.groups
query.explanation: A named capture such as `(?<name>a)` is recorded on the match object `groups` property. `match.groups.name` is `"a"`. The name is not only a numbered slot, and `groups` is present when the pattern has a named group.

questions.prompt: `toSpliced` returns a new array and does not mutate the receiver.

query.title: toSpliced copies instead of mutating
query.explanation: `toSpliced` returns a new array with the splice applied and does not change the receiver. `a[1]` stays `2` while the copy has `9` at that index. It is the copying form of `splice`, which would have mutated `a`.

questions.prompt: `toReversed` returns a new array and does not mutate the receiver.

query.title: toReversed copies instead of mutating
query.explanation: `toReversed` returns a new array in reverse order and leaves the receiver in place. `a[0]` stays `1` and `b[0]` is `3`. It is the copying form of `reverse`, which would have mutated `a`.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` omits symbol-keyed properties and does not throw because of them.
questions.code:
const s = Symbol("s");
JSON.stringify({ a: 1, [s]: 2 });

query.title: JSON.stringify skips symbol keys
query.explanation: Symbol keys are not JSON data, so `JSON.stringify` omits them and returns `"{\"a\":1}"`. Their presence does not throw. A bigint value would throw, but a symbol key is skipped instead.

questions.prompt: A proxy `get` trap receives the proxy as the receiver when the property is read on the proxy.

query.title: The get trap receiver is the proxy
query.explanation: Reading a property on a proxy calls the `get` trap with the proxy as the receiver. That receiver is the proxy object, not the target. The trap does not receive the target in the receiver slot just because the value lives there.

questions.prompt: A `has` trap that reports a non-configurable existing target property as absent throws TypeError.

query.title: A has trap cannot hide a non-configurable property
query.syntax: "a" in proxy; // TypeError when has returns false
query.explanation: If the target already has a non-configurable property, the `has` trap must report it as present. Returning false makes the `in` check throw a TypeError. The trap cannot pretend the property is absent.

questions.prompt: Public instance class fields are enumerable.

query.title: Public instance fields are enumerable
query.explanation: A public instance field is an enumerable own data property, so `Object.keys` lists `n`. Class methods are the non-enumerable ones. The field is not hidden the way a method on the prototype is.
